source_text: κὸς εἰς τὸ ἄναλκί τε καὶ ἀδρανὲς, οὐκ ἂν γένοιτό πως ἐν εὐκαρπίᾳ πολλῇ, καθάπερ ἀμέλει καὶ τὰ γηράσκοντα τῶν φυτῶν, παλαιουμένης αὐτῶν τῆς ῥίζης, κατοκνοῦντα φαίνεται πρὸς τὴν ὡρίμων ἐκβολήν. Οὐκοῦν ὁ δίκαιος ἀληθῶς καὶ φιλοικτίρμων Θεὸς, ἀναλόγως ταῖς ἑκάστου προθυμίαις, καὶ τῇ κατὰ νοῦν ἐπιτηδειότητι, δέχεται τοὺς καρποὺς, οὔτε τὸ ἄναλκι καὶ ἀφηβηκὸς, ἔξω τε λόγου τιθεὶς, καὶ ἀποπέμπων ὡς ἀδρανὲς, οὔτε μὴν ἀγέραστον τὸ εὐσθενὲς ἀνιεὶς, ἀνευρύνων δὲ ὥσπερ τοῖς ἐθέλουσι τὸ εὐδοκιμεῖν, καθ' ὃν ἂν ἕκαστος ἔχοι τρόπον. Τοὺς δέ γε τὴν ἕξιν ἀσθενεστέρους, τάχα δέ που καὶ ὀλιγογνώμονας, αὐτὸς ἕξει, τὴν καρποφορίαν ἐπιμετρῶν ἑκάστῳ τὸ κατ' ἰσχύν. Τοῦτο γὰρ, οἶμαι, ἐστὶ τὸ, «Στήσεται ἐναντίον τοῦ ἱερέως, καὶ τιμήσει αὐτὸν ὁ ἱερεὺς, καθ' ὅσον ἰσχύει ἡ χεὶρ τοῦ εὐξαμένου.» {ΠΑΛΛ.} Ὡς ἰσχνὸς ὁ λόγος! {ΚΥΡ.} Ἀνακομιστέον δὴ οὖν, ὦ Παλλάδιε, τῷ Θεῷ, καθάπερ ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας, καὶ ὀφλημάτων ἐν τάξει, πολιτείαν ἁγιοπρεπῆ, καὶ τῆς ἐξαιρέτου ζωῆς τὰ αὐχήματα. Γεγραφότος δὲ δὴ τῶν ἁγίων διεπύθου τινὸς, «Τίμα τὸν Κύριον ἀπὸ σῶν δικαίων πόνων, καὶ ἀπάρχου αὐτῷ ἀπὸ σῶν καρπῶν δικαιοσύνης.» Βουθυσίαις μὲν γὰρ οἱ πάλαι καὶ λιβανωτοῖς ᾤοντο τιμᾷν· πολιτείας γὰρ ἥδε τῆς κατὰ νόμον ὁδός· ἡμεῖς δὲ λοιπὸν οἱ ἐν Χριστῷ διὰ πίστεως, τὴν ἀμείνω καὶ προφερεστέραν ἰόντες τρίβον, τὴν ἐν πνεύματί τε καὶ ἀληθείᾳ προσκύνησιν ἀναθήσομεν τῷ Θεῷ, πάντα μὲν ὥσπερ σείοντες κάλων, εἴς γε τὸ δύνασθαι γεννικῶς διαπεραίνειν ἃ χρῆν, ἀναθήμασι δὲ τοῖς πνευματικοῖς τε καὶ ἱεροῖς καταγεραίρειν Θεόν. Φημὶ γὰρ ἔγωγε διαμεμνῆσθαι δεῖν λέγοντος ἐναργῶς διὰ τοῦ πανσόφου Μωσέως, «Τὰ ἐκπορευόμενα διὰ τῶν χειλέων σου φυλάξῃ,» τουτέστιν, ὅπερ ἂν εὔξῃ, διαπεραίνειν ἐπείγου καὶ μάλα γοργῶς. Χρῆμα γὰρ ἐν τούτοις ὁ μελλησμὸς οὐκ ἀζήμιον. «Ἐὰν γὰρ εὔξῃ, φησὶν, εὐχὴν τῷ Κυρίῳ, μὴ χρονίσῃς τοῦ ἀποδοῦναι αὐτήν· ἀγαθὸν τὸ μὴ εὔξασθαί σε, ἢ εὔξασθαι καὶ μὴ ἀποδοῦναι.» {ΠΑΛΛ.} Ἀληθές. {ΚΥΡ.} Καὶ μέντοι τῆς εὐτεχνίας τὸν εὐφυᾶ σκοπὸν, τῆς ἐπί γε τῷ δεῖν ἀποπεραίνειν εὐχὰς καὶ ὁμολογίας, ἀναμάθοι τις ἂν οὐχ ἑτέρωθεν ἀπλανῶς, πλὴν ὅτι διὰ τοῦ νόμου. Γέγραπται γὰρ, ὅτι «Λύχνος τοῖς ποσί μου ὁ νόμος σου, καὶ φῶς ταῖς τρίβοις μου.» Ἢ γὰρ οὐχὶ νόμῳ τῷ θείῳ φωταγωγούμεθα, καὶ οἶμον ὀρθήν τε καὶ ἀπλανῆ διᾴττοι τις ἂν, λύχνον ὥσπερ τινὰ τὰς ἐκεῖθεν ἔχων αὐγάς;» {ΠΑΛΛ.} Πῶς γὰρ οὔ; Ψάλλει γάρ που καὶ ὁ θεσπέσιος Δαβίδ· «Ἡ ἐντολὴ Κυρίου τηλαυγὴς, φωτίζουσα ὀφθαλμούς.» {ΚΥΡ.} Τίνα δὴ οὖν τρόπον εὐδοκιμήσομεν, τὸν εὐκλεᾶ τε καὶ πάναγνον διαζῶντες βίον, καὶ λαμπρὸν ἀνάθημα τῷ Θεῷ, τοὺς τῆς ἄγαν ἐπιεικείας ἀπονέμοντες τρόπους, εἴσῃ τοι καὶ μάλα σαφῶς, καὶ δι' ἑτέρων ἡμῖν θεσπισμάτων ἐπισκήπτοντος τοῦ Θεοῦ.
pass_a_gloss: Cyril (continuing): ...[what has sunk into the feeble and powerless] would not be in much fruitfulness (εὐκαρπία), just as aging plants (φυτῶν), their root (ῥίζα) growing old (παλαιουμένης), appear hesitant (κατοκνοῦντα) toward the putting forth (ἐκβολή) of ripe things. So the truly just (δίκαιος) and pity-loving (φιλοικτίρμων) God, in proportion (ἀναλόγως) to each one's eagernesses (προθυμίαις) and fitness (ἐπιτηδειότης) of mind, receives (δέχεται) the fruits, neither placing outside account (ἔξω λόγου) and sending away as powerless the feeble and past-prime (ἀφηβηκός), nor letting the strong go unrewarded (ἀγέραστον), but as it were widening (ἀνευρύνων) for the willing the being approved (εὐδοκιμεῖν), in whatever way each may have. Those weaker in condition (ἕξις), perhaps also of little understanding (ὀλιγογνώμονας), he himself will have (αὐτὸς ἕξει), measuring out (ἐπιμετρῶν) to each the fruit-bearing (καρποφορία) according to strength (ἰσχύν). This, I think, is: 'He shall stand before the priest, and the priest shall value (τιμήσει) him according as the hand of the one who vowed (εὐξαμένου) is able' [Lev 27:8]. Palladius: How subtle/fine (ἰσχνός) the account! Cyril: We must bring up (ἀνακομιστέον) to God, as an odour of fragrance (ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας) and in the rank of debts (ὀφλημάτων), a holy-befitting citizenship/way of life (πολιτεία ἁγιοπρεπής) and the boasts (αὐχήματα) of the exceptional (ἐξαιρέτου) life. You learned from one of the saints who wrote: 'Honor the Lord from your just labors (πόνων), and offer firstfruits (ἀπάρχου) to him from your fruits of righteousness (δικαιοσύνης)' [Prov 3:9]. Those of old thought to honor with ox-sacrifices (βουθυσίαις) and frankincense (λιβανωτοῖς); for this was the road of the way of life according to law. But we now, those in Christ through faith, going the better and superior path (τρίβον), will dedicate (ἀναθήσομεν) to God the worship (προσκύνησις) in Spirit and truth [John 4:23-24], as it were shaking every rope (πάντα σείοντες κάλων, proverb: 'making every effort'), to be able nobly (γεννικῶς) to accomplish what is needed, and to honor (καταγεραίρειν) God with spiritual and sacred dedications. For I say we must remember him saying clearly through the most wise Moses: 'You shall keep (φυλάξῃ) what goes out through your lips' [Deut 23:24 LXX = 23:23], that is, whatever you vow, hasten (ἐπείγου) to accomplish, and very quickly (γοργῶς). For in these matters delay (μελλησμός) is a thing not without loss (ἀζήμιον). 'If you vow a vow to the Lord, he says, do not delay (μὴ χρονίσῃς) to pay (ἀποδοῦναι) it; it is good that you not vow rather than vow and not pay' [Eccl 5:3-4 LXX = 5:4-5]. Palladius: True. Cyril: The well-natured aim (εὐφυᾶ σκοπόν) of the good skill (εὐτεχνία) concerning the need to complete vows (εὐχάς) and confessions/pledges (ὁμολογίας) one would learn unerringly (ἀπλανῶς) from nowhere else except through the law. For it is written: 'A lamp (λύχνος) to my feet is your law (νόμος), and a light to my paths' [Ps 118:105 LXX = 119:105]. Or are we not light-guided (φωταγωγούμεθα) by the divine law, and could one not dart along (διᾴττοι) a straight and unerring road (οἶμον), having its rays (αὐγάς) like a lamp? Palladius: How not? For the inspired David sings: 'The commandment (ἐντολή) of the Lord is far-shining (τηλαυγής), enlightening (φωτίζουσα) eyes' [Ps 18:9 LXX = 19:8]. Cyril: In what manner we will be approved (εὐδοκιμήσομεν), living through the glorious and all-pure (πάναγνον) life, and rendering (ἀπονέμοντες) as a bright dedication (λαμπρὸν ἀνάθημα) to God the ways of great goodness (ἐπιεικεία), you will know very clearly, God enjoining (ἐπισκήπτοντος) us also through other oracles (θεσπισμάτων).
pass_b_english: Cyril: …could hardly be very fruitful, just as aging plants, when their root grows old, are seen to be slow in putting forth ripe fruit. So God, who is truly just and loves to show compassion, accepts the fruits in proportion to each person’s zeal and capacity of mind. He neither disregards what is feeble and past its prime, sending it away as powerless, nor lets the strong go without reward; rather he opens wide, as it were, the way for those who are willing to win his approval, in whatever manner each is able. And those who are weaker in their condition, and perhaps also of little understanding, he himself will keep, measuring the fruit he asks of each by his strength. For this, I think, is the meaning of: ‘He shall stand before the priest, and the priest shall value him according to what the one who vowed can afford’ (Leviticus 27:8).

Cyril: So, Palladius, we must offer to God, like a sweet fragrance and as a debt we owe, a way of life fitting for saints and the glories of an outstanding life. You have learned from one of the saints, who wrote: ‘Honor the Lord from your just labors, and offer him firstfruits from your fruits of righteousness’ (Proverbs 3:9). For the people of old thought they honored him with sacrifices of oxen and with frankincense, since that was the road of life under the law. But we, who are now in Christ through faith, are going by the better and more excellent path, and we shall offer God worship in spirit and truth (John 4:23–24), making every effort, as it were, to be able to carry out nobly what we ought, and honoring God with spiritual and holy offerings. For I say that we must remember him who speaks plainly through the most wise Moses: ‘You shall keep what goes out through your lips’ (Deuteronomy 23:23). That is, whatever you vow, hasten to carry it out, and very promptly. For in such matters delay is not without loss. ‘For if you make a vow to the Lord,’ it says, ‘do not delay in paying it’ (Deuteronomy 23:21; Ecclesiastes 5:4). ‘It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay’ (Ecclesiastes 5:5).

Cyril: Indeed, there is a wise aim in the art of fulfilling vows and pledges as we ought, and one could learn it without error from no other source than the law. For it is written: ‘Your law is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths’ (Psalm 119:105). Or are we not guided by the light of the divine law, and could one not speed along a straight road that never strays, with its rays as a kind of lamp?
Palladius: Of course. For the inspired David also sings somewhere: ‘The commandment of the Lord is radiant, giving light to the eyes’ (Psalm 19:8).

Cyril: You will learn very clearly how we shall win approval, living a glorious and wholly pure life and rendering to God, as a splendid offering, the ways of great goodness, for God gives us his charge through other oracles too.

anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of De adoratione Book 16. Translated afresh from the PG 68 Greek on 2026-10-23; the withdrawn English was not used for wording.

apparatus.note: PG OCR; a column may cut mid-sentence or mid-word.
αὐτὸς ἕξει is abrupt and the text may be faulty; rendered by the sense of the context ('he himself will keep').

PG 68.1040. Opens mid-sentence from §15 (‘what has already declined into feebleness…’). αὐτὸς ἕξει (‘He himself will have/hold’) is abrupt; rendered ‘He himself will keep’, meaning he keeps them in his acceptance; the text may be faulty. Palladius’s Ὡς ἰσχνὸς ὁ λόγος praises the argument as finely drawn (ἰσχνός, ‘slender, subtle’), not as weak. ‘Fragrant aroma’ (ὀσμὴ εὐωδίας) is stock sacrificial language (Leviticus passim; compare Ephesians 5:2, Philippians 4:18); no single verse is meant, so it is uncited. Proverbs 3:9 matches the LXX word for word. ‘Worship in Spirit and truth’ is the phrase of John 4:23–24 that gives the whole work its title. πάντα σείοντες κάλων is a proverb (‘shaking out every rope’), rendered by its sense ‘making every effort’. ‘You shall keep what goes out through your lips’: LXX Deuteronomy 23:24 = English Deuteronomy 23:23. The next quotation, introduced only by ‘it says’ after a mention of Moses, matches LXX Ecclesiastes 5:3–4 (μὴ χρονίσῃς τοῦ ἀποδοῦναι αὐτήν; ἀγαθὸν τὸ μὴ εὔξασθαί σε…) = English Ecclesiastes 5:4–5. The first clause blends LXX Deuteronomy 23:22 (= English 23:21: ἐὰν δὲ εὔξῃ εὐχὴν κυρίῳ, ‘if you vow a vow to the Lord’) with Ecclesiastes (μὴ χρονίσῃς τοῦ ἀποδοῦναι), so both are cited; the second sentence is Ecclesiastes 5:5 alone. LXX Psalm 118:105 reads ὁ λόγος σου (‘your word’); Cyril’s text has ὁ νόμος σου (‘your law’), and the English follows Cyril. ‘The commandment of the Lord is radiant’: LXX Psalm 18:9 = English Psalm 19:8. ἐπιείκεια rendered ‘goodness’ (moral excellence), its usual sense in Cyril. Lev 27:8 ‘the hand of the one who vowed’ is the Hebrew idiom for means; rendered ‘what the one who vowed can afford’.
